item.title: Staff Post - Wikiwalk Proposal
item.content:encoded:
Timer Expired. Edits made as discussed below. Author may revert at any time.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

You know what's worse than ever expanding clay? Ever expanding clay that's been fused with, and is under the control of, a militaristic piece of play-doh (aka SCP-705). The Foundation would likely want to keep these two squishy skips separate. As such, I am recommending the following edits:

Changing this:

SCP-837 is to be stored in its fully factored state when not undergoing experiments, with each factor stored in a separate plastic container. All experiments should be conducted in rooms with reinforced flooring.

To this:

SCP-837 is to be stored in its fully factored state when not undergoing experiments, with each factor stored in a separate plastic container. All experiments should be conducted in rooms with reinforced flooring.

Due to potentially dangerous consequences of cross-contamination, at no point are SCP-705 and SCP-837 to be stored at the same site.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.content:encoded:
I don't see the world-destroying potential, am I missing something?

Yes, we could theroetically generate an infinite number of 1 dram bits. Unlimited tons of clay for whatever purpose we care to think of. But when things get out of control, the carefully measured dividing containers get busted up, those bits are going to get pushed back together by gravity and their own weight, and the mass vanishes again.
Long before we have a mass of clay that could take out a city, much less threaten the world, the problem would solve itself back down to about 368 kilograms.

If you take eight 1201-dram sized pieces, and one 769-dram sized piece, and combine them, the resulting mass of clay will have mass equal to Earth and a 3.68 times larger volume. The components needed to enact this particular XK scenario weigh less than 20kg, can be stored anywhere, and don't require any special skills or even knowledge of their anomalous properties to be combined.

I love this article.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Someone file this under "simple, yet effective" as a shining example thereof.

I was thinking about it today, about how you could take, say, a five-dram piece and start peeling off infinite one-dram pieces. And then you could take those one-dram pieces and combine them back together and still only have one dram.

And now I just realized that you can take infinite one-dram pieces off of a one-dram piece.

I am quite honestly freaking out about a block of clay. You deserve extra upvotes.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Excellent! Straight to the point, no tacked-on danger, no action-packed addenda, no staff hi-jinks; just a solidly weird thing that messes with our assumptions about reality. Good job.

Put one dram in a device that alternately pushes the clay past some wire cutters and then smooshes it back together. Balance the device on a pulley system with a counter-weight greater than one dram, but lighter than the post-cutter mass. The constant up-and-down can be eaisly tapped for electricity generation. Close the loop and have the divider/smoosher device powered by the system.

With good design, and assuming we can meet some critical threshold for mechanical efficiency, we have not only a perpetual motion machine, but possibly infinite free power.
